data.title: Trump hosts gala for meme coin investors as his token plunges to record lowsÂ
data.description:
[NEW YORK] US President Donald Trump has made hundreds of millions from his $TRUMP meme coin, but at a Sunday (Nov 22) dinner for the token’s biggest holders, he said his motive for supporting the cryptocurrency was to boost the economic competitiveness of the United States.

“I’m doing it for the United States... If we don’t do it, China’s going to do it,” Trump told attendees at his golf club outside Washington.

It was the third time Trump had held a gala for the top owners of his meme coin, which once soared as high as US$75 but has fallen to a record low of under US$1.

The private dinner this year was more low-key than the initial event last year, attendees said, with a smaller crowd and far less money at stake this time. Attendees qualified for the dinner based on their time-weighted holdings of the $TRUMP coin from Sep 30 to Nov 16.

Organisers indicated that 185 crypto wallets met the criteria for Sunday’s dinner, although the leaderboard on the $TRUMP coin club website listed just 130 wallets when the contest concluded on November 16.

Together, those listed wallets only held US$8.6 million – a shadow of the US$148 million listed for the dinner in May 2025, which was attended by 220 wealthy crypto investors.

Sunday’s participants stood in the rain as they waited to enter the Trump National club in Sterling, Virginia. Attendees described the scene inside as subdued.

It was a far different atmosphere from the first gala, when tuxedo-clad contest winners pulled up to the club in luxury sports cars, and protesters chanted and stomped outside the club as the presidential Marine One helicopter descended.

The May 2025 event’s biggest $TRUMP holder was China-born crypto billionaire Justin Sun, who had US$18.5 million of the token. This time, there was no Sun at the event signing autographs.

Attendees were able to dine on grilled filet mignon and pan-seared halibut while hearing speeches from the likes of Kevin O’Leary of the Shark Tank television show and NBA veteran Tristan Thompson.

According to the contest’s website, the top 29 winners would join a VIP reception with the president and receive a gift bag with Trump swag. The top four also would get an 18-karat gold Trump-branded watch.

Morten Christensen, founder of cryptocurrency platform Airdrop Alert, said he qualified for the top 29 with US$41,000 of time-weighted $TRUMP holdings by using a hedging strategy – buying and selling the token using perpetual futures – that ensured he did not lose any money.

But he was denied a VIP band at the event, Christensen said.

“I asked like five people from the staff” and was told to email customer support, he said on Sunday night.

“Obviously, no one is going to reply right now,” said Christensen, who added that he was kicked out of the event around 7 pm for “sharing with the press.”

He waited outside in the rain for his sister, who was still inside.

The Trump Meme Coin project and the White House did not respond to requests for comment.

Meme coin tumbles

More than half of the digital wallets publicly listed on the contest leaderboard for Sunday’s dinner are tied directly to crypto exchanges that bar US-based users, indicating they are linked to foreign nationals, according to an analysis of blockchain data prepared for Reuters by the nonpartisan, nonprofit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen.

The Trump family’s other crypto-connected equities and ventures have also fallen in value to record lows. Together, outside investors in their five main crypto and crypto-linked projects have lost more than US$5 billion, according to a Reuters analysis.

But the $TRUMP token has earned the Trump family itself at least US$635 million, according to the president’s June financial disclosure statement.

In total, the Trumps had earned at least US$2.3 billion through April from their four main crypto ventures, including the meme coin.

The president’s stake in a fifth crypto-linked venture, Trump Media & Technology Group, is worth about US$430 million. REUTERS

data.title: AI agents and stablecoins a âperfect matchâ for payments, says MetaCompâs Tin Pei Ling
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The rise of agentic payments is creating a new era where finance can “think, act and settle” autonomously at the same time, but capturing this opportunity safely is key, said Tin Pei Ling, co-president of payments company MetaComp. 

She described programmable money and agentic artificial intelligence as “almost like a perfect match”, with stablecoins enabling round-the-clock settlement while AI agents can independently initiate and optimise transactions at speed.

But as institutions begin allowing AI agents to execute financial transactions, concerns have emerged over increased risks such as fraud, Tin told The Business Times. 

“These (concerns) are valid, but at the same time this shouldn’t stop us,” she said, highlighting the need for clear regulations alongside tools and technology to help enforce them.

Tin cited MetaComp’s approach to developing regulatory technology solutions such as VisionX, a compliance system that monitors risk across both traditional fiat databases and blockchain ledgers.

To govern autonomous AI transactions, the company also launched the StableX Know Your Agent Framework in April, which is a governance framework that defines an AI agent’s registered identity, authority and accountability.

“In today’s context, a lot of things are retrospective, which means that transactions may have already happened. Then you sample, check and take action if there’s something wrong,” said Tin, who is also a Member of Parliament.

“Technology has allowed us to be a bit more preemptive and proactive as opposed to retrospective.”

Agentic infrastructure for Asean

Founded in 2018, MetaComp connects fiat and stablecoin payment rails through what it calls a Web2.5 architecture, combining blockchain technology with existing financial architecture.

The company, which holds a Major Payment Institution licence from the Monetary Authority of Singapore, said on Nov 17 that it is scaling its StableX Agentic Network to carry more cross-border payments into and across South-east Asia, for banks, payment service providers and businesses.

The network is designed for payments made by agents and humans, with governance built into how they take part, said MetaComp.

Through this network, institutions can pay out in local currency in six Asean markets: Singapore, Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam, the Philippines and Thailand. They can also collect local currency in Singapore, the Philippines and Indonesia, with Vietnam to follow. 

Tin noted that settlement times for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) making cross-border payments can take days using traditional payment rails. 

“If their cash is being locked up because it cannot settle, (SMEs) cannot receive it in time. Then further downstream, they cannot pay their suppliers or for other things, and that could represent quite a significant opportunity cost,” she said. 

Stablecoins have been able to address this challenge, said Tin. “It’s not to replace the good old Swift (Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication), per se, but at least (to) offer a compelling alternative.” 

MetaComp is seeing demand for its payment solutions, particularly among advanced tech, AI and med-tech companies based in Singapore and North Asia, said Tin.

“As these firms expand their footprints into emerging markets, they require a trusted payments partner with versatile, cross-border capabilities to manage overseas suppliers and buyers.” 

The company said in March that it raised US$35 million across two funding rounds within three months, drawing backing from investors including Alibaba.

Its latest capital injection is being used to deepen capabilities across its StableX Agentic Network and secure regulatory approvals to expand payment corridors across Asia, the Middle East, Africa and Latin America, noted Tin.

The agentic network is designed for payments made by agents and humans, with governance built into how they take part.

Since November 2025, the company said its network has grown to over 1,000 members, reaching more than 100,000 users. Based on a press release, MetaComp has an annual transaction volume run rate of US$14 billion for FY2026 and was full-year net profitable in 2025.

Global coordination

Tin stressed that as agentic finance matures, robust domestic frameworks will need to be matched by global alignment.

“The genie is already out of the bottle; no point wishing it away. So we better make sure that the governance, the safety, and all the interventions that we need to make are ready,” she said.

Over the next year, international coordination will be critical to prevent fragmented standards across different platforms and institutions.

Tin echoed sentiments shared by Singapore Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan at the United Nations on Sep 26, calling for a unified framework convention on AI safety.

“If we leave it to institutions, it will be very slow because there will be competition and there could even be distrust among each other,” Tin said.

“How do we make sure that we level up and are interoperable? Who should be setting the standards? If there is an international body that can coordinate this, then that’s a different story.”

Tin, who entered the financial industry in 2023, said the rapid pace of technological change has created opportunities for newcomers in the industry.

“In fintech, things are moving really fast. There are always new technologies, solutions and ideas that emerge, and that actually levelled the playing field,” she said.

“Everyone is trying to keep up, to learn, and to see how to make the best out of this.”

data.title: Stocks to watch: Keppel Infrastructure Trust,  Elite UK Reit, Thakral, Katrina
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Nov 20):

Keppel Infrastructure Trust (KIT) : KIT secured S$200 million in revolving loan facilities, with outstanding loans immediately repayable if its trustee-manager ceases to be wholly owned by Keppel Capital and/or Keppel, or ceases to act as KIT’s trustee-manager and a replacement wholly owned by the Keppel companies is appointed beforehand. Neither trigger had occurred yet, but if either leads to cross defaults, about S$1.9 billion in total facilities could be affected. The counter ended 1 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.50 on Thursday, before the news.

Elite UK Reit : The manager of the real estate investment trust (Reit) submitted a planning application for a 352-bed student accommodation development in Wales. It expects a decision in 2027 and aims to start demolition and construction in 2028, subject to approval. The counter ended 1.7 per cent or £0.005 lower at £0.295 on Thursday, before the news.

Thakral : Thakral is selling its remaining 6.1 per cent stake in The Beauty Tech Group (TBTG), netting S$56.5 million, and expects to record a S$17.9 million gain over its end-June book value of S$38.6 million. Including the partial sale at TBTG’s initial public offering last year, the investment returned about S$70 million in cash to Thakral. The group plans to use the latest proceeds for new investments, its existing businesses and other capital needs. Shares of Thakral ended flat at S$1.45 on Thursday, before the announcement.

Katrina Group : An entity linked to carmaker BYD raised its stake in the F&B operator to 13.09 per cent from 4.91 per cent after buying more than 21 million shares for S$500,000 in an off-market transaction. It became a substantial shareholder in September, when it acquired a 5 per cent stake by buying 12.6 million shares from Katrina’s CEO for S$299,880. Shares of Katrina ended 8.3 per cent or S$0.003 higher at S$0.039 on Thursday, before the news.

data.title: Singapore, China reach 29 deals at top bilateral forum
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore and China have concluded 29 deals in the areas of trade and finance, science and technology, and public health at the end of their top bilateral forum on Nov 23.

Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong, who co-chairs the forum with Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang, said the breadth of the discussions reflects how the two countries’ partnership have continued to evolve.

A key distinguishing trait of the Singapore-China relationship has always been the ability to stay relevant and forward-looking through different phases of the countries’ development, he said in his closing remarks after the Joint Council for Bilateral Cooperation (JCBC) series of meetings.

“Even as circumstances change, both sides have continued to adapt, build on our complementary strengths and find new areas of practical cooperation,” said Gan. 

Singapore and China take turns hosting the JCBC, which is in its 22nd edition. This year’s talks lasted more than two hours at the Shangri-La Singapore.

The 29 deliverables announced are the highest in recent years. In 2025, the JCBC held in the south-western Chinese city of Chongqing resulted in 27 deals. In 2024, 25 agreements were reached in Singapore. 

Elaborating on this year’s agreements, Gan said both sides renewed a memorandum of understanding on trade in services which will bring opportunities for companies to work with one another, and for consumers to tap healthcare, eldercare, professional, legal and other services.

In finance, he said a fast payment systems linkage for small-value payment transfers - which could boost commerce and tourism numbers - is under discussion. 

“This will complement the growing range of renminbi payment channels between our countries, and make it easier for our people and businesses in Singapore to access the Chinese market.”

In public health, agencies from both countries signed a new agreement that will facilitate mutual exchanges and learning, he added.

Singapore officials who attended the JCBC included Minister for Education Desmond Lee, Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo and Minister for National Development Chee Hong Tat.

Ding was flanked by top Chinese officials such as Deputy Secretary General of the State Council Wang Yang, Vice-Minister of Foreign Affairs Hua Chunying and Cao Zhongming, China’s Ambassador to Singapore. THE STRAITS TIMES

data.title: Consider lowering homeownership barriers for some non-resident foreigners
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore has a high homeownership rate; about nine in 10 resident households own their homes.

However, people living and working here who are not Singapore citizens or permanent residents face huge obstacles when buying a home.

A non-PR foreigner buying any home pays 60 per cent additional buyer’s stamp duty (ABSD). ABSD does not apply to a citizen buying a first home, while a PR first homebuyer pays 5 per cent ABSD.

ABSD is paid in addition to buyer’s stamp duty, which is progressive and ranges from 1 to 6 per cent for homes.

The Republic is open to skilled foreign professionals; this enhances its attractiveness as a location for high value-add activities, and in turn supports better job opportunities for Singaporeans.  

The Employment Pass (EP) allows foreign professionals, managers, executives and technicians to work here. 

As at June 2026, there were 204,300 EP holders, up from 203,300 as at December 2025. Among the EP holders are people who have been living here for several years or more, and have not been able to secure PR status. 

In perspective, a PR buying a first home for S$2 million pays ABSD of S$100,000, while an EP holder purchasing a home of similar value may have to pay ABSD of S$1.2 million.

Lower ABSD rates

Should transaction costs for EP holders buying homes here be lowered? Perhaps, for first home purchases, levy ABSD of 10 per cent on EP holders who have held such status for over three consecutive years.

Singapore is competing for high-quality foreign talent, especially in fast-growing or critical parts of the economy where there is a shortage of talent.

Letting an EP holder buy a home here without facing swingeing transaction costs could enhance the Republic’s attractiveness to skilled foreigners.  And the stickiness from owning a home might better anchor EP holders to the country. 

Moreover, it would appear fair for an EP holder – who has spent multiple years here – to not face far higher transaction costs than a PR, when buying a first home here for owner occupation.

Importantly, too, some non-PR foreigners buying a first home here for investment might not pay any ABSD. 

Under respective free trade agreements (FTAs), nationals and PRs of Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland as well as US nationals are accorded the same stamp duty treatment as Singapore citizens.

In short, a US citizen buying a first home here need not incur ABSD, for example.

Should EP holders from other countries pay much higher transaction taxes on first home purchases than nationals of the above countries with FTAs?

An EP holder who spends around S$6,000 a month in housing rent would incur about S$864,000 in rental expenses over 12 years. Using some or all of these funds to help buy a home here instead, should transaction costs not be punitive, can be enormously helpful to the said EP holder.

Over a 12-year period between Q3 2014 and Q3 2026, the Urban Redevelopment Authority’s property price index of private homes rose by about 50 per cent, while the rental index of private homes islandwide climbed by around 43 per cent.

HDB ownership restrictions

Another key difference in the housing market between PRs and non-PR foreigners is in Housing & Development Board (HDB) flat ownership.

For example, a couple comprising partners who have held PR status for at least three years can buy a HDB resale unclassified or standard flat, excluding 3Gen flats, whereas non-PR foreigner households cannot own HDB flats.

Consider allowing a couple, both EP holders, who have held such status for at least three years, to buy HDB resale unclassified or standard flats excluding 3Gen units. Perhaps, apply a resale levy to said EP holders when they sell their HDB units.

Having PR and other foreigner households live within HDB estates can possibly help such households better assimilate with Singaporeans.

Also, consider expanding public housing options for couples comprising a Singapore citizen and a non-PR foreigner.

Numerous Singapore citizens marry non-PR foreigners. In 2025, the number of marriages involving a citizen and a non-resident foreigner was 5,909. There were marriages involving a citizen and 4,189 non-resident brides, as well as 1,720 non-resident grooms.

Currently, subject to meeting various criteria, a couple comprising a Singapore citizen and a non-PR foreigner who holds a valid work pass or visit pass, and is hoping to buy a new HDB flat, is restricted to buying a two-room flexi unit.

In this case, the citizen looking to purchase a new HDB flat must be at least 35 years old. New HDB flats, unlike resale units, are sold at subsidised prices.

Possibly, lower the age requirement to buy a new HDB flat for a Singapore citizen who marries a non-resident foreigner spouse. Also, subject to meeting various criteria, let a couple comprising a citizen and a non-resident buy larger new HDB flats.

A larger two-room flexi flat is about half the size of a four-room flat. The former has one bedroom, while the latter has three bedrooms.

Rightly, housing policies here prioritise Singapore citizens over PRs and PRs over non-PR foreigners.

Indeed, a key perk for a rich foreigner becoming a Singaporean is the right to buy a home here cost-effectively. A newly minted citizen can buy a landed property including a detached house in a Good Class Bungalow Area. Ownership of landed homes, meanwhile, is generally restricted to Singapore citizens.  

Hopefully, the Republic draws foreigners to become PRs and citizens, for reasons beyond just gaining Singapore citizenship or PR status which offers a cost-effective way to homeownership in safe haven Singapore.  

Having foreigners who become Singaporeans because they treasure and contribute to the nation’s multiculturalism, social cohesion, rule of law, strong work ethic and economic dynamism among others would be great.

Meanwhile, let us be more welcoming to non-resident foreigners such as EP holders, and those who marry Singaporeans by easing homeownership barriers for EP holders, as well as couples comprising a citizen and a non-resident spouse.

data.title: Indiaâs Tata Steel moves to control APL Apollo with US$1.67Â billion stake buy, open offer
data.description:
INDIA’S Tata Steel said on Monday (Nov 23) it will acquire an initial 26.38 per cent stake in APL Apollo Tubes for about 155.11 billion rupees (US$1.67 billion) to expand its downstream steel business, a day after agreeing to sell its tubes and colour-coated steel businesses to APL Apollo.

The steelmaker will acquire the stake at 2,100 rupees per share, a 1 per cent discount to APL Apollo’s closing price on Friday.

Tata Steel will also launch a mandatory open offer to acquire an additional 26 per cent of APL Apollo at 2,301.4 rupees per share, for up to 167.56 billion rupees.

Shares of APL Apollo slumped 10 per cent, while Tata Steel dropped 4 per cent.

The transactions will give Tata Steel control of India’s largest structural steel tubes maker and expand its presence in colour-coated steel and tubes.

Tata Steel said it expects the deals to lift the share of downstream businesses in its portfolio to about 53 per cent from 35 per cent.

“This strategic move helps to consolidate the Steel Tubes and the Colour Coated business under Tata Steel’s ownership while unlocking multiple synergies between the two companies,” Tata Steel CEO and managing director T V Narendran said in a statement.

Colour-coated steel is treated with protective coatings to improve resistance to corrosion and is commonly used in roofing and construction.

The combined business will initially have a capacity of 7.5 million metric tons a year, which Tata Steel plans to expand to 15.5 million tons by 2035, including about 9 million tons of steel tubes and 6.5 million tons of colour-coated products.

Separately, APL Apollo agreed on Sunday to acquire Tata Steel’s tubes business and its entire stake in Tata Steel Colors for up to 280 billion rupees in cash.

APL Apollo will initially fund the purchase through acquisition financing and later replace the debt with longer-term capitalisation, Tata Steel said. REUTERS

data.title: Stocks to watch: Yangzijiang Shipbuilding, Seatrium, Frencken
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 19):

Yangzijiang Shipbuilding : The shipbuilder’s subsidiary has entered into an investment agreement with China’s Taicang Port Economic and Technological Development Zone. The agreement is in relation to a project to develop a clean energy vessel intelligent manufacturing base in Taicang city, located in Jaingsu province. The group expects capital expenditure for the project to be about 3.38 billion yuan (US$507 million). Shares of Yangzijiang Shipbuilding ended 1.6 per cent or S$0.07 higher at S$4.39 on Wednesday, before the announcement.

Seatrium : The offshore, marine and energy specialist reported that its net order book stood at S$12.2 billion as at end-September, comprising 35 projects with deliveries extending through 2033. It had secured S$1.7 billion in new orders so far this year. Seatrium expects its underlying net profit for FY2026 to be materially higher than in FY2025. The counter ended 0.6 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$1.71, before the news.

Frencken : The technology manufacturer announced on Wednesday (Nov 18) a 31.3 per cent year-on-year increase in earnings to S$13 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30. Revenue grew 12.8 per cent to S$238.5 million, from S$211.5 million a year earlier. The increase was mainly driven by Frencken’s mechatronics division’s revenue, which rose 13.4 per cent to S$214.3 million. The counter ended S$0.01, or 0.6 per cent, up at S$1.71 before the news.

data.title: Stocks in Asia drop again as local regulators rush to stem rout
data.description:
SOUTH Korean and Chinese shares fell as a global technology stock rout intensified, testing Asian authorities’ efforts to restore investor confidence as the AI trade unravelled.

The benchmark Kospi Index dropped as much as 4.4 per cent, following Friday’s losses on Wall Street that sent the S&P 500 into a technical correction and the Nasdaq 100 posting its worst week since March 2020. Korea has trimmed the year’s rally, which at one point reached more than 110 per cent, to just 10 per cent.

Shares in mainland China and Hong Kong also fell over 1 per cent after Monday’s opening bell. Taiwanese stocks fluctuated. 

The declines extended Friday’s rout in Asia that later spread to other regions. That prompted regulators in Korea, Taiwan and China to announce measures — from buying equities to widening short-selling curbs — over the weekend to stabilise markets as the profitability of AI trades from chipmakers to hyperscalers gets drastically repriced. 

Anthropic PBC’s slide after its much-anticipated debut is emblematic of the turn in sentiment, with investors piling into US Treasuries and other haven assets.

“These interventions are circuit breakers rather than a turning point,” said Dilin Wu, a strategist at broker Pepperstone Group. “These steps may help stabilise prices in the near term, but they can’t reverse a broader reassessment of AI valuations or bring foreign investors back on their own.”

Korean authorities said on Sunday they will ease daily limits on company share buybacks for three months and begin preparations to activate a stock-market stabilisation fund if needed. The rescue fund was last used during the global financial crisis in 2008, according to local media.

Taiwan expanded curbs on short sales of local stocks on Saturday and said it has been buying shares, stepping up efforts to revive confidence after the island’s benchmark index had its worst weekly fall in 35 years.

The local Financial Supervisory Commission imposed a blanket ban on short selling below the previous trading day’s closing price, covering both margin short sales and borrowed shares.

Separately, the island’s NT$500 billion (US$15 billion) National Financial Stabilisation Fund said it has entered the market to support Taiwanese stocks and urged investors to remain confident.

In China, the minimum margin requirement for investors buying securities with borrowed funds will fall to 80 per cent from 100 per cent on Nov 30, according to notices issued on Sunday by the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing stock exchanges with approval from the China Securities Regulatory Commission. The exchanges had raised the ratio to 100 per cent from 80 per cent in January to curb leverage risks. 

Regulators said the latest adjustment is related to a marked decline in margin-financing activity and relatively low overall leverage. Brokerages can apply the revised rules to outstanding financing contracts when calculating available margin balances, while investors engaged in abnormal trading may face stricter requirements and other risk controls.

The change could unleash nearly 400 billion yuan (US$60 billion) in additional funds, the Xinhua News Agency reported on Sunday, citing the regulator.

Meanwhile, the Shenzhen Stock Exchange is proposing introducing market makers on the ChiNext board, according to draft rules released for public comment. The system is intended to broaden the pool of market participants, improve liquidity and pricing efficiency, and strengthen the market.

“The support measures appear more sentiment- and liquidity-oriented than fundamentally market-changing,” said Fu Zhifeng, chief investment officer at Shanghai Chengzhou Investment Management.

“The market-making measure may provide only marginal liquidity support, while lowering the minimum margin requirement for securities financing from 100 per cent to 80 per cent mainly eases near-term forced-selling pressure and provides investors more time to meet margin calls, rather than bringing meaningful new capital into the market.”

The moves add to a series of efforts by Beijing to restore confidence after a months-long rout pushed the benchmark CSI 300 Index into a bear market.

The gauge tumbled over 8 per cent in October, its worst monthly performance in more than a decade, as weakness in the economy and a sharp reversal in tech shares weighed on sentiment. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Nvidiaâs slump, Anthropicâs listing turn spotlight on Big AIâs need for new governance frameworks
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] When news of Jensen Huang’s extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive broke earlier this month, it surprised me that many observers seemed to think he had finally crossed the line.

It was already clear by then that Huang had also been having an affair with a woman US authorities believed was a Chinese spy, and that he had misrepresented the nature of that relationship to senior officials at Nvidia for some time.

In my view, this was objectively much worse than an illicit dalliance with a subordinate. The alleged spy was linked to a major buyer of Nvidia chips in Singapore called Megaspeed, which had ties to Chinese companies. This naturally alarmed the US government, and has already led to tighter restrictions on Nvidia.

Last week, the US Commerce Department announced licence requirements for the export of advanced artificial intelligence chips for use in data centres providing remote computing power to China. Licence requirements were also slapped on the export of advanced AI chips to destinations with “unacceptable risk of diversion” – including Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brazil and Thailand.

These restrictions and the ouster of Huang – who had advocated for China to be allowed access to AI chips, and provided buyers of AI chips with financial support – have felt like a supply shock for the booming technology sector.

Nvidia’s shares sank a further 22.9 per cent last week, despite the company reporting robust third-quarter financial numbers and strong revenue guidance for 2027. Since the end of last month, when the spy scandal began making headlines, Nvidia’s shares have slumped 38.7 per cent.

The S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 have fallen 8.8 per cent and 11.8 per cent, respectively, during the same period.

“Indispensable” CEOs

To be clear, I’m not suggesting that Huang should be excused for his affairs with employees of Nvidia – it later emerged that there was more than one.

Illicit relationships with customers, business partners or subordinates are effectively undisclosed conflicts of interests that have the potential to harm a company and its stakeholders. One might also argue that such lapses reveal character flaws that make CEOs unsuited for their roles.

Certainly, cultural attitudes towards this sort of behaviour seem to have become less forgiving. In recent years, major companies such as Nestle, BP, McDonald’s and Intel have given their CEOs the boot for relationships with subordinates.

Yet, Huang’s involvement with the alleged Chinese spy clearly had the potential to cause far more damage to Nvidia and its stakeholders than his affairs with employees – not least by putting all of them in the crosshairs of the US government.

This case is also perplexing as Huang’s exit from Nvidia appears to have weakened confidence in the company and wider AI ecosystem. Many investors, technology sector luminaries as well as Nvidia’s own employees are now calling for Huang’s return.

Nvidia has said it is not considering inviting Huang back.

The way I see it, market regulators and corporate governance experts should begin thinking hard about how seemingly indispensable corporate leaders such as Huang can be effectively checked; and how to ensure fast-growing companies in important new fields do not betray their stakeholders.

Anthropic’s share classes

Part of the answer may come from the big AI companies themselves. Anthropic, for one, had some interesting things to say during the run-up to its initial public offering.

In a letter to prospective investors, the company’s founders extolled the potential of AI to boost productivity and accelerate the pace of medical breakthroughs, while also warning of the immense harm the technology may inflict on humanity.

“AI has unusually large externalities, both positive and negative. Cultivating the positive externalities, and defending against the negative ones, is to some degree in tension with the natural incentives of a for-profit company, and with the standard governance structure of a publicly traded company,” the founders said.

To address this, Anthropic was formed as a public benefit corporation, which requires its board to weigh the interests of its shareholders against its public benefit mission and the interests of those materially affected by its conduct.

Within that structure, different groups of stakeholders are accorded influence and interest through five different classes of shares.

Most of the control lies with holders of its Class F and Class T shares. The single Class F share, held by an entity controlled by Anthropic’s seven co-founders, has 50.1 per cent voting power.

On the other hand, an independent body called the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), holds Anthropic’s single Class T share, giving it the power to appoint four of the seven members of the company’s board.

Anthropic will also issue Class E shares to its non-founder employees over time, giving them a say on some governance matters – including the appointment of one Class T director under certain circumstances.

All the economic benefits of the company belong exclusively to holders of its Class A and Class N shares, though. The difference between the two is that the Class N shares have no voting rights, except where required by law.

The Class N shares are held by Anthropic’s public benefit fund and some strategic partners, such as Amazon and Alphabet. The company plans to contribute 2 per cent of its equity to its public benefit fund for every sustained 50 per cent increase in its share price.

The Class N shares convert to Class A shares when transferred by their holders to non-affiliated parties.

Improve standard practices

Investors who resisted the introduction of dual-class shares in Singapore may well be appalled by Anthropic’s multiple share classes.

Not only will Anthropic’s founders maintain majority voting power even if they dispose of their shares, the trustees of the LTBT may appoint directors opposed to the company maximising its profits. Holders of the Class A shares will also face dilution from the ongoing issue and conversion of Class N shares.

However, Anthropic’s founders pointed out in their letter that the size and structure of the company’s plan to allocate equity to its public benefit fund is “not outside the range” of executive compensation packages at some companies.

It may also be desirable, in my view, for independent bodies of various stripes to have some influence over corporate behemoths that bestride the world.

Anthropic may be more aware of its own power than many other companies in the same league, because of the nature of its business and the fact that it has garnered a US$1.5 trillion valuation within only six years of its founding.

By contrast, Nvidia attained a market capitalisation of US$1 trillion only in 2023, three decades after it began operating. While its CEO Huang should be proud of his achievement, his stunning fall from grace is perhaps a sign that the company needs to be run differently now.

Anthropic’s novel governance framework may well not be the answer, of course – indeed, the company itself says it is a work in progress. Yet, its attempt to improve on standard corporate practices is probably something other companies should emulate as they grow and evolve.

“We will make mistakes, and we expect to learn from others as much as they learn from us. If our competitors adopt our practices and improve on them, we consider that a success,” its founders said.
